audits.title: Retrospective on my unsupervised elicitation challenge
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly a challenge retrospective, not an experiment report, but it describes in real detail how crowd-submitted self-check and best-of-N strategies all failed on Opus 4.6 before a newer model solved the task.
experiments: Crowd-submitted elicitation strategies (self-check, best-of-N) on Opus 4.6 for the Ancient Greek accent exercise
audits.primary_experiment: Crowd-submitted elicitation strategies (self-check, best-of-N) on Opus 4.6 for the Ancient Greek accent exercise

hypothesis.evidence: Poses the challenge as a question (can the model be made to do it) and believes Opus 4.6 holds the knowledge, but states no expectation about the strategies.

claim_scope.evidence: One textbook fill-in-the-blank accent exercise, a bit over 20 crowd submissions, mostly self-check or best-of-N, scoped to Opus 4.6.

method.evidence: Asking the model to double-check its work, generating many attempts and having it pick the best, plus extended thinking; translate-back used to show the model knows the rules.

models.evidence: Claude Opus 4.6 (main), Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.4 Pro.

result_direction.evidence: No Opus 4.6 submission succeeded, and the author impression is that these strategies did slightly worse than the raw prompt.

failure_type.evidence: Author calls the blindness to accents somehow unexplained, offers only an unproven guess (model in learner mode) and cannot see how to test it.

quote.value: No submission that used Opus 4.6 was successful

audits.notes: Retrospective of a crowd challenge; failed attempts were by participants, not the author; test exercise and answers withheld.

audits.title: I was Wrong, Simulator Theory is Real
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly a corrected, positive result, but it explains in detail how an earlier study showed a flat null because of a message-role bug.
experiments: Original study run with a message-role bug (assistant turns sent as system), showing no effect of prior wrong answers
audits.primary_experiment: Original study run with a message-role bug (assistant turns sent as system), showing no effect of prior wrong answers

hypothesis.evidence: Hypothesis 1: more earlier wrong answers in context means more wrong answers; Hypothesis 2: effect grows with flattery. Simulator theory predicts rising errors.

claim_scope.evidence: Defines variables (error rate, prior wrong answers up to about 10, ten prompt supplements) but gives no question set, sample sizes or model.

method.evidence: Wrong answers placed in earlier turns via OpenAI ChatCompletion API, varying their number and a prompt supplement; statistical tests on the outcomes.

models.evidence: Only an unnamed LLM called through the OpenAI ChatCompletion API; no model name is given.

result_direction.evidence: With the bug, the error rate stayed essentially flat as prior wrong answers increased; the fixed run reversed this.

failure_type.evidence: Author found and fixed a message-role bug that flattened the data; the bug is confirmed, so suspected is only the closest available label.

quote.value: with the bug, Y was basically flat

audits.notes: Original null result was a message-role bug; fix reverses it. Plots hold the data; model unnamed.

audits.title: Why LLMs Aren't Scientists Yet.
audits.genuine_reason: Main content is four autonomous research attempts by LLM agents, three of which failed in implementation or evaluation, with documented failure modes.
experiments: Autonomous AI-scientist pipeline on four research ideas (three failed in implementation or evaluation)
Semantic entropy as a black-box jailbreak detector
Differentiable tree search planner collapsing into a simple actor-critic
audits.primary_experiment: Autonomous AI-scientist pipeline on four research ideas (three failed in implementation or evaluation)

hypothesis.evidence: States only a goal (see how far LLMs get toward autonomous research with little scaffolding); no expectation or prediction about the outcome.

claim_scope.evidence: Six Gemini-based agents plus Claude Code, four ideas from a 135-plus-paper corpus across three subdomains, no ablations, failures observed qualitatively.

method.evidence: Six role-specific agents (idea, hypothesis, planning, evaluation, revision, outline) sharing a file system, Claude Code implementing; zero-shot reviewer filtering of ideas.

models.evidence: Gemini 2.5 Pro (all six agents), Claude Code (implementation and writing).

result_direction.evidence: Three of four ideas failed during implementation or evaluation; one AI safety idea completed the pipeline and was published.

failure_type.evidence: Failures are attributed to six agent failure modes (drift, context loss, overexcitement and others), which fit no single schema type.

quote.value: Of these four, three failed during implementation or evaluation

audits.notes: Crosspost summary of a longer report; per-failure detail is in the report. The semantic entropy result lacks models.

audits.title: Does Circuit Analysis Interpretability Scale? Evidence from Multiple Choice Capabilities in Chinchilla
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly a positive scaling result, but it reports that the nth-item explanation of the correct-letter heads was only partial and messy on randomized labels.
experiments: Explaining correct-letter head semantics with an nth-item-in-enumeration feature, tested on randomized answer labels
audits.primary_experiment: Explaining correct-letter head semantics with an nth-item-in-enumeration feature, tested on randomized answer labels

hypothesis.evidence: States aims (test scaling, understand head semantics) but no prior expectation; only a later personal guess that circuits are messy at all scales.

claim_scope.evidence: Chinchilla 70B, multiple-choice answer-letter circuit, correct-letter attention heads, normal versus randomized answer labels; dataset and sample sizes not stated in the post.

method.evidence: Direct logit attribution, activation patching, attention pattern visualization, query/key/value subspace compression, and label mutation experiments (random letters or numbers, shuffled ABCD).

result_direction.evidence: Authors call results mixed: the head subspaces compress without loss on normal labels, but the nth-item explanation is only partial on randomized labels.

failure_type.evidence: Post says only that more remains to learn about these heads; separate guess that such circuits are messy at every scale.

quote.value: we find that it is only a partial explanation

audits.notes: Cross-post of paper abstract and summary; failure part is brief, detail is in the arXiv paper; figures omitted.

audits.title: Evaluating What 2026 Looks Like So Far
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly a human grading of old predictions with a positive verdict, but it details a second experiment where o3-mini resolved predictions much worse than the human grader.
experiments: Automated resolution of predictions (correctness and difficulty scores) with o3-mini
Automated extraction of predictions from text with o3-mini
audits.primary_experiment: Automated resolution of predictions (correctness and difficulty scores) with o3-mini

hypothesis.evidence: Only says the author tried to see whether o3-mini could automate the process; a question, with no stated expectation beforehand.

claim_scope.evidence: o3-mini on 2022 and 2023 predictions only (model cutoff), no web search, chunks up to 1000 tokens, compared with human grading by the post author.

method.evidence: Two-pass prediction extraction prompts, chunked input, then scoring each prediction for correctness (0 to 2) and difficulty (1 to 5) using the Arb rubric.

result_direction.evidence: Extraction looked promising; resolution was mediocre, with mean correctness gap of 0.75 on a 0 to 2 scale and difficulty gap of 0.83.

failure_type.evidence: Author blames crude technique and missing web search, and plans multi-step flows with search and multi-model averaging; closest available label.

quote.value: the results are substantially worse than human evaluations

audits.notes: Mostly a positive human grading of predictions; the o3-mini automation is the failed part; results partly in figures.

audits.title: Classifier Context Rot: Monitor Performance Degrades with Context Length
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly a positive finding that monitors degrade with long context, but it describes in detail two fine-tuning mitigations that did not transfer or got worse.
experiments: Fine-tuning GPT-4.1 on synthetic needle data and on proxy-task logs to fix long-context monitor degradation
Periodic reminders to the monitor after each tool call
audits.primary_experiment: Fine-tuning GPT-4.1 on synthetic needle data and on proxy-task logs to fix long-context monitor degradation

hypothesis.evidence: Fine-tuning is described as something tried; no stated expectation for it, apart from a general remark that better post-training might help.

claim_scope.evidence: GPT-4.1 fine-tuned via OpenAI API at 65k-token context on two dataset types, tested on needle injection and prepended MonitorBench; sizes not given.

method.evidence: Fine-tuning on synthetic one-line attacks inserted into real transcripts, and on algorithmically generated logs with an approval policy.

result_direction.evidence: Synthetic needle data helped a lot on needle injection but not significantly on prepended MonitorBench; proxy task helped slightly on needles but hurt MonitorBench.

failure_type.evidence: Author thinks in-distribution gains likely come from making the model notice out-of-place bash calls, so these datasets would not help real monitors.

quote.value: on prepended MonitorBench performance did not increase statistically significantly

audits.notes: Mostly a positive finding; fine-tuning section is the failure. Results sit in figures; padding-evasion finding is attack-adjacent.

audits.title: My Minor AI Safety Research Projects (Q3 2025)
audits.genuine_reason: A roundup of small projects, mostly not experiment reports, but one project (steering with an uppercaseness direction) is described as failing on an instruct model.
experiments: Uppishcase: steering with an uppercaseness direction to control prompt salience
audits.primary_experiment: Uppishcase: steering with an uppercaseness direction to control prompt salience

hypothesis.evidence: Author proposed that steering along an uppercaseness direction could give continuous control over instruction salience, and early results looked promising.

claim_scope.evidence: No model names, training data, or scale given; says only that a more advanced instruct model failed and a second attempt used a residual-stream direction.

method.evidence: Uppercaseness direction from token embeddings with per-token steering via a Hugging Face hook; second attempt learned a residual-stream direction from training data using TransformerLens.

models.evidence: None named; only an unnamed more advanced instruct model is mentioned.

result_direction.evidence: On the more advanced instruct model, any steering reduced text salience, the reverse of the intended effect; second attempt gave similar, confusing results.

failure_type.evidence: Author only presumes out-of-distribution activations made text hard to read; second attempt gave confusing plots; the right intervention is still unknown.

quote.value: any steering at all reduced the salience of text

audits.notes: One of three small projects; failed part is brief, no numbers or model names; code linked on GitHub.
